newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria govt seeks delay in preparing '97 budget.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria govt seeks delay in preparing '97 budget.

text.p: Bulgaria's cabinet has asked parliament to extend the deadline for presenting the 1997 budget draft by two months while it clarifies what macroeconomic parameters to work from.

"The government wants the deadline extended to December 31 because the programmes (for bank stabilisation and liquidation of loss makers) it is carrying out will cause large changes in macroeconomic indicators," the cabinet said in a letter to the parliamentary chairman obtained by Reuters on Friday.
The letter coincides with a visit by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission in Sofia to review the government's reform performance and work out a budget framework for next year.

Under the Budget Law the government had to submit the 1997 budget draft to parliament for approval at least two months before the beginning of the new fiscal year, which in Bulgaria coincides with the calendar year.
However, Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov has not yet presented a draft to the cabinet.
Another reason for the delay was the need to match expected proceeds from privatisation in 1996 with government targets in the draft, the letter said.
The government hopes to raise some $1 billion from the planned privatisation of some 20 large firms to stave off default on Bulgaria's foreign debt.
Record high interest rates in the past two months also deterred the government from meeting the deadline because they made domestic debt payments unaffordably high, officials said.

Bulgaria's central bank, under pressure from the government to ease lending, on Thursday cut its main interest rate to 15 percent monthly from 20 percent, or 180 percent annually from 240 percent, to become effective on Monday.
Also on Thursday the central bank opened insolvency suits against another eight banks, bringing their total number to 13.
Fulfilment of government pledges to close down loss-makers, speed up privatisation and stabilise the banking sector is seen as a key to releasing a twice-delayed $115 million IMF credit.
Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said earlier this week the macroeconomic situation could hinder the IMF talks.
Gross domestic product is now expected to fall by between 8.1 percent and 10.5 percent this year against zero growth targeted in the 1996 budget.
By the end of September Bulgaria had already topped annual macroeconomic targets laid out in the 1996 budget which was revised for the first time in July.

Cumulative inflation for the first nine months hit 153 percent against an annual target of 105 percent while the Bulgarian lev fell to 244 to the dollar on Friday against a projected exchange rate of 190 levs per dollar.
